intended_object: The interval-arithmetic product of two closed intervals with dyadic endpoints, [a,b]·[c,d] = [min{ac,ad,bc,bd}, max{ac,ad,bc,bd}], computed with a sign-based case split. Inferred from the docstring and from comparing it with the neighbouring `IntervalDyadic.mul`.
explanation:
The definition is meant to compute the same interval as the four-product `IntervalDyadic.mul`, only faster. Dyadic multiplication here is exact: mantissas multiply and exponents add, with no rounding.

I checked each of the eight sign cases against the exact product interval:
- I ≥ 0, J ≥ 0: [I.lo·J.lo, I.hi·J.hi].
- I ≥ 0, J ≤ 0: [I.hi·J.lo, I.lo·J.hi].
- I ≥ 0, J straddles 0: [I.hi·J.lo, I.hi·J.hi].
- I ≤ 0, J ≥ 0: [I.lo·J.hi, I.hi·J.lo].
- I ≤ 0, J ≤ 0: [I.hi·J.hi, I.lo·J.lo].
- I ≤ 0, J straddles 0: [I.lo·J.hi, I.lo·J.lo].
- I straddles 0, J ≥ 0: [I.lo·J.hi, I.hi·J.hi].
- I straddles 0, J ≤ 0: [I.hi·J.lo, I.lo·J.lo].

In each case these are exactly the min and the max of the four endpoint products. When both intervals straddle 0, it falls back to the full min4/max4 product.

So the definition computes exactly the interval product, and it is faithful. The dyadic setting is the point of this computational, verified-arithmetic construction, so it is not too narrow. Mathlib has no counterpart: `NonemptyInterval`'s multiplication is componentwise and is only correct for canonically ordered (nonnegative) settings, not signed intervals.
